title: Question 7
stem:
A $\beta^-$ particle from a radioactive source is travelling in a vacuum with kinetic energy $460\text{ eV}$. The particle enters a uniform electric field at a right-angle and follows the path shown in Fig. 7.1.

{{figure:figure_7_1}}

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: The direction of the electric field is in the plane of the paper. On Fig. 7.1, draw an arrow to show the direction of the electric field.
hints: Hint 1: Look at which way the path bends in Fig. 7.1 and remember a $\beta^-$ particle is negatively charged, so the force on it acts opposite to the field direction.
parts.proper_answer: Electric field arrow points vertically downwards in the plane of the paper, opposite to the upward deflection.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link bending to force**
You can see the $\beta^-$ particle bends upwards once inside the field. That tells you the electric force $F$ on it must have an upward component.

Step 2: **Use the negative charge**
For any charge, $$F = qE$$ in vector terms. A $\beta^-$ particle is an electron with charge $q = -e$, so force is opposite to field. To get an upward force, the field $E$ must point downwards. So draw a downward arrow inside the shaded region.

key_concepts: force on negative charge in electric field
relation between field direction and deflection

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the $\beta^-$ particle before it enters the electric field.
hints: Hint 1: Start by identifying what a $\beta^-$ particle is and what mass to use, and notice the kinetic energy is given in eV not in SI units.
Hint 2: Think about how kinetic energy is linked to mass and speed for a particle moving much slower than light.
Hint 3: Remember to first convert $460\text{ eV}$ to joules using $1\text{ eV} = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ J}$, then rearrange for $v$ before substituting numbers.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Identify the particle and energy**
A $\beta^-$ particle is a fast electron, so $m = 9.11 \times 10^{-31}\text{ kg}$. Its kinetic energy is given as $460\text{ eV}$. Electronvolts must be changed to joules for use with $m$ in kg.

Step 2: **Convert eV to joules**
$$E_k = 460 \times 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ J}$$ $$E_k = 7.36 \times 10^{-17}\text{ J}$$

Step 3: **Rearrange kinetic energy for speed**
For non-relativistic motion: $$E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$$ $$v = \sqrt{\frac{2E_k}{m}}$$ $$v = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 7.36 \times 10^{-17}}{9.11 \times 10^{-31}}}$$ $$v = 1.3 \times 10^7\text{ m s}^{-1}$$ to 2 s.f. This is well below the speed of light, so the classical formula is fine.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
Other $\beta^-$ particles from the same radioactive source travel outside the electric field along the same incident path as that shown in Fig. 7.1.

State and briefly explain whether those $\beta^-$ particles will all follow the same path inside the electric field.
hints: Hint 1: Recall what you know about $\beta^-$ decay - do all emitted electrons share the total decay energy in the same way, or is the energy shared with another particle?
Hint 2: Think about how a faster or slower particle entering the same transverse field would be deflected differently because of the time spent in the field.
parts.proper_answer: No, they will not follow the same path. $\beta^-$ particles from the same source have a range of kinetic energies and speeds, so they experience the electric force for different times and are deflected by different amounts.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Remember beta energies are not all the same**
In $\beta^-$ decay the available energy is shared randomly between the $\beta$ particle and an antineutrino. That gives a continuous spectrum of kinetic energies, not a single value. So other particles will have different speeds from $1.3 \times 10^7\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

Step 2: **Link speed to path in the field**
The transverse deflection depends on the acceleration $a = F/m = eE/m$ and the time spent in the field, which depends on entry speed. A slower particle spends longer in the field and deflects more, a faster one deflects less. Therefore with various speeds they follow different curved paths.
